triage.label: Self-care
triage.action: This can usually be managed at home

workup: Refer if vision affected or pupil abnormal

triage.label: See a doctor soon
triage.action: Book an appointment in the next few days

conditions.summary: Insulin resistance causing sustained high blood glucose. Thirst, passing large volumes of urine, fatigue, blurred vision and recurrent infections, often for months.

exam.positive: Prodrome of nausea, warmth and tunnel vision
Excludes orthostatic hypotension
Normal; a murmur suggests structural disease

conditions.name: Vasovagal syncope

triage.label: Routine
triage.action: Discuss with your doctor at a routine appointment

conditions.summary: A reflex drop in heart rate and blood pressure, typically after standing a long time, pain, heat or the sight of blood. Warning nausea and greying vision come first.

exam.step: Lying and standing blood pressure at 1 and 3 minutes
exam.positive: A drop of 20 systolic or 10 diastolic confirms
Antihypertensives, diuretics, alpha blockers, antidepressants
Volume depletion is a common contributor

conditions.name: Orthostatic hypotension

triage.label: Routine
triage.action: Discuss with your doctor at a routine appointment

conditions.summary: Blood pressure falls on standing, so the brain is briefly underperfused. Common in older people, on blood pressure tablets, or when dehydrated.

exam.step: Test for relative afferent pupillary defect
exam.positive: Swinging light test positive in optic neuritis

exam.positive: Red desaturation precedes acuity loss
Upper motor neurone pattern
Cerebellar signs

conditions.summary: Immune attack on the insulation of nerve fibres. Discrete episodes of visual loss, numbness or weakness lasting weeks, separated in time and in body region.

exam.positive: Circumcorneal injection, deepest at the limbus
Small, irregular and poorly reactive

exam.positive: Blurred disc margins with loss of venous pulsation

exam.positive: Enlarged blind spot

conditions.name: Orbital cellulitis

triage.label: Emergency
triage.action: Call emergency services or go to an emergency department now

exam.positive: Lens opacity
Quantifies functional impact to guide surgical timing

conditions.name: Cataract

triage.label: Routine
triage.action: Discuss with your doctor at a routine appointment

conditions.summary: Gradual, painless blurring of vision, glare/haloes around lights (especially at night), and colours appearing faded -- typically over months to years, more common with age. India performs a very high volume of cataract surgery nationally; sudden vision loss or pain is NOT cataract and should be worked up separately.
workup: Clinical slit-lamp examination showing lens opacity
Visual acuity testing to quantify functional impact
No medical treatment slows cataract progression
Cataract surgery (phacoemulsification with lens implant) is curative and done once vision impacts daily function

exam.positive: Quantifies the refractive error and the correction needed

conditions.name: Refractive error

triage.label: Self-care
triage.action: This can usually be managed at home

conditions.summary: Blurred vision at distance (myopia), near (hyperopia/presbyopia) or both, sometimes with headache/eye strain from uncorrected focusing effort -- extremely common at any age, and by far the most common cause of 'blurred vision' in day-to-day practice. New or rapidly changing refractive error, especially in a diabetic, should prompt a check for a treatable underlying cause rather than just a new prescription.
workup: Refractive surgery (LASIK etc.) as an elective option for suitable candidates

exam.positive: Microaneurysms, haemorrhages, exudates, or neovascularisation depending on stage

exam.step: Ask specifically about diabetes control and duration
exam.positive: Longer duration and poorer control both raise risk

conditions.name: Diabetic retinopathy

triage.label: Routine
triage.action: Discuss with your doctor at a routine appointment

conditions.summary: Often asymptomatic in early stages, which is why screening matters; later stages cause blurred or patchy vision loss, floaters, or sudden vision loss from vitreous haemorrhage or retinal detachment. Given India's very large and growing diabetic population, this is a major cause of preventable blindness. Sudden vision loss or a shower of new floaters in a known diabetic needs same-day ophthalmology assessment.
workup: Dilated fundoscopy or retinal photography -- the annual screening standard for all diabetics
OCT/fluorescein angiography if advanced disease is found
Tight glycaemic, blood pressure and lipid control slows progression
Laser photocoagulation or anti-VEGF injections for sight-threatening disease

exam.positive: Often raised, but a meaningful proportion of chronic open-angle glaucoma has only mildly raised or normal IOP -- a real nuance, not a clean rule-out test on its own

exam.step: Ask specifically whether the eye is painful or red
exam.positive: Classically neither -- a painless, white eye is the key distinguishing feature from acute angle-closure glaucoma, which is the opposite on both counts

exam.step: Formal visual field testing and optic disc examination
exam.positive: Peripheral field loss and optic disc cupping are the actual diagnostic findings -- no dedicated evidence node captures peripheral vision loss directly here, so this is assessed on formal testing rather than the patient's own description

labs.confirms: Supportive but not always raised -- see the nuance above

labs.test: Formal visual field testing (perimetry) and optic disc imaging
labs.confirms: The actual diagnostic findings for glaucoma -- peripheral field loss and characteristic disc cupping

conditions.name: Chronic open-angle glaucoma

triage.label: See a doctor soon
triage.action: Arrange an appointment in the next day or two

conditions.summary: A slowly progressive, classically PAINLESS optic nerve disease with a white (not red), comfortable eye -- the exact opposite presentation to acute angle-closure glaucoma, which shares this bundle. Vision loss begins in the peripheral field and is often unnoticed by the patient until advanced, since the brain compensates -- no dedicated 'peripheral/tunnel vision' evidence node exists here, so this is assessed on formal visual field testing rather than the patient's own description of blur. Genuinely the most common form of glaucoma, far more common than the acute presentation, and a leading cause of irreversible blindness worldwide precisely because it is silent until late -- routine eye pressure screening after age 40, not waiting for symptoms, is the point.
workup: Intraocular pressure (IOP) measurement -- though a meaningful fraction of cases have only mildly raised or even normal IOP ('normal-tension glaucoma'), so a normal reading does not exclude it
Formal visual field testing -- detects the characteristic peripheral field loss well before the patient notices it
Optic disc examination/imaging for characteristic cupping
Topical IOP-lowering eye drops (prostaglandin analogues first-line)
Laser trabeculoplasty or surgery if drops are insufficient

exam.step: Ask about distortion of straight lines (metamorphopsia) and difficulty with fine central detail, with peripheral vision preserved
exam.positive: The genuine hallmark of AMD -- not captured by a dedicated node in this checker, an important disclosed limitation

exam.step: Ask specifically about halos around lights and eye pain, looking for their ABSENCE
exam.positive: Halos suggest a lens/glare phenomenon (cataract) rather than a retinal one, and AMD itself is genuinely painless -- their presence should prompt reconsidering another cause

exam.step: Ask about a history of diabetes and check whether blood sugar control is a factor
exam.positive: AMD is not a diabetes-driven disease -- a significant diabetes history should prompt considering diabetic retinopathy instead

labs.confirms: Shows characteristic drusen and pigmentary changes at the macula
The definitive investigation, distinguishing dry from wet (neovascular) AMD and guiding treatment

conditions.name: Age-related macular degeneration

triage.label: Routine
triage.action: Discuss with your doctor at a routine appointment

conditions.summary: Gradual, progressive damage to the macula (the central part of the retina responsible for sharp, detailed central vision), the leading cause of irreversible central vision loss in older adults. DISCLOSED GAP: no evidence node in this catalogue captures AMD's actual hallmark feature (central scotoma or metamorphopsia -- straight lines appearing wavy or distorted), a genuine, honestly disclosed limitation. Modelled here through generic gradual blurred vision with a strong age-skew, plus negative discriminators against Cataract (no halos -- a lens/glare phenomenon, not retinal), Chronic Glaucoma (normal eye pressure) and Diabetic Retinopathy (not diabetes-driven), all sharing this bundle.
workup: Ask specifically about DISTORTION of straight lines and difficulty with fine central detail (reading, faces) with preserved peripheral vision -- the genuine hallmark, though not captured by a dedicated node here
Refer for dilated fundus examination and optical coherence tomography (OCT) to confirm the diagnosis and distinguish dry from wet (neovascular) AMD
AREDS2-formula vitamin/mineral supplementation (vitamin C, E, zinc, copper, lutein, zeaxanthin) for intermediate AMD, shown to reduce progression risk
Urgent same-week ophthalmology referral for sudden new distortion or a rapid drop in central vision -- possible wet AMD, which needs prompt anti-VEGF injection therapy to preserve vision

redFlags.label: Possible sepsis
redFlags.message: A fever together with confusion, very fast breathing, mottled skin or a collapsing blood pressure can mean infection is affecting the whole body.
redFlags.action: Call emergency services now. Do not wait to see whether it settles.

redFlags.label: Rash that does not fade under pressure
redFlags.message: Spots that stay visible when a glass is pressed on them, alongside feeling unwell, can be a sign of bacteria in the bloodstream.

redFlags.label: Possible severe allergic reaction
redFlags.message: Swelling of the throat or tongue with difficulty breathing after a food, sting, or medicine can close the airway within minutes.
redFlags.action: Use an adrenaline auto-injector if you have one, then call emergency services.

redFlags.label: Reduced consciousness
redFlags.message: Being difficult to rouse, or drifting in and out of awareness, always needs immediate assessment whatever the cause.
redFlags.action: Call emergency services now. Place the person on their side if unresponsive.

redFlags.label: Possible stroke
redFlags.message: Sudden facial drooping, arm weakness or difficulty speaking is a stroke until proven otherwise. Treatment works only within a few hours.
redFlags.action: Call emergency services now and note the exact time symptoms began.

redFlags.label: Seizure
redFlags.message: A first seizure needs assessment to find the cause and to advise on driving and safety.
redFlags.action: Seek urgent assessment today. Call emergency services if the seizure lasted over five minutes or a second one followed.

redFlags.label: Significant gastrointestinal bleeding
redFlags.message: Vomiting blood, or passing black tarry stools, means bleeding inside the digestive tract.
redFlags.action: Go to an emergency department now.

redFlags.label: New jaundice
redFlags.message: Yellowing of the skin or eyes always needs blood tests to find out why.

redFlags.label: Sudden loss of vision
redFlags.message: Sight lost suddenly in one or both eyes needs assessment the same hour, whatever the cause.
redFlags.action: Go to an eye emergency department now.

redFlags.label: Thoughts of self-harm
redFlags.message: Thoughts of harming yourself or of being better off dead deserve help today. You do not have to be in crisis to reach out.
redFlags.action: Contact your doctor, a crisis line, or go to an emergency department now. If you are in immediate danger, call emergency services.

redFlags.label: New confusion coming on over hours or days
redFlags.message: Confusion that has come on over hours or days, or that comes and goes through the day, is delirium until proven otherwise. It is caused by something else -- an infection, a drug, pain, retention -- and that cause needs finding today.
redFlags.action: Seek same-day medical assessment. Take a list of all medications. Call emergency services if they are drowsy, feverish or cannot be roused properly.

disclaimer: This tool provides information about possible causes of symptoms. It is not a diagnosis and it cannot examine you. It does not replace assessment by a qualified clinician. If you feel very unwell, or your symptoms are getting rapidly worse, seek medical help immediately regardless of what this tool says.
